title: Learn by Copy: how Jason Cohen learned to write by copying others' style, not their words
summary: Jason Cohen argues that copying style (not plagiarizing) is one of the best ways to learn a craft and discover your own voice. He shows how copying Seth Godin and James Altucher taught him what he likes and can do, and applies the same idea to racquetball, chefs and Picasso.

principles.text: Copy style, not words: imitating how others do things is a legitimate way to learn, as long as it's a means to an end.
principles.quote: Rather, copying is one of the best ways of learning, growing, evaluating, and exploring. It's a valid tool so long as we regard it as a means to an end.

principles.text: Imitation reveals what you like and what you're actually able to do, which is how you find your own voice.
principles.quote: By copying I learned what I liked, what I had some ability to do.

principles.text: Try on other people's approaches like clothes; keep the bits that fit you and discard the rest.
principles.quote: The way to discovering who you are, what you value, what you're good at, what you believe, is to try things on, like clothes, to see what fits.

principles.text: Keep experimenting with other styles even after you've found your voice; the goal is growth, not matching the master.
principles.quote: "being as good as James at James' style" is not the goal. The goal is to learn and grow as a writer, and this was fun to do.

principles.text: Copying works in any pursuit: watch the best performers and mimic their specifics until you absorb what works.
principles.quote: I learned by watching the good players and trying to copy their movements--their swing, where they'd run, where they'd place the ball.

principles.text: Copying a style teaches concrete lessons about your own preferences, such as wanting a framework rather than only inspiration.
principles.quote: I like evocative examples, but I don't like leaving the reader without a framework for finding a solution.
